challenges.title: Read the Room
challenges.description: Every good hacker reads the code. Your first flag is hidden in plain sight. Inspect this page's HTML source and find the hidden comment.
challenges.learningObjective: Learn to use browser Developer Tools and read HTML source code

hints.text: Open your browser's Developer Tools (F12 or right-click → Inspect). Go to the 'Sources' tab or 'Elements' tab and look at the page's HTML.
Search for 'flag' in the HTML using Ctrl+F. Look for HTML comments (they look like <!-- text --> in the code).

solutionSteps: 1. Right-click on this page → 'Inspect' or press F12
3. You'll find a comment like: <!-- flag{n0_w3bsit3_s3cr3ts} -->
4. Copy the flag and submit it

pythonScript.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import re

# Solution for Challenge 1: Read the Room
# This script fetches a webpage and looks for flag patterns

with open('page.html', 'r') as f:
    html = f.read()

# Search for flag pattern in HTML comments
flags = re.findall(r'<!--\s*(flag\{[^}]+\})\s*-->', html)

if flags:
    print(f"Flag found: {flags[0]}")
else:
    print("No flag found. Check if the page has HTML comments.")
pythonScript.explanation: Simple regex to find flags hidden in HTML comments. This teaches file I/O and regular expressions.

challenges.title: Say Cheese!
challenges.description: Cameras store metadata in photos. Extract EXIF data from a JPEG image file. The flag is hidden in the photo's comment field.
challenges.learningObjective: Understand EXIF metadata, learn to use Python Pillow library, extract hidden data from images
challenges.prerequisite: Python 3 with Pillow installed: pip install Pillow

hints.text: EXIF stands for 'Exchangeable Image File Format'. It stores camera info, GPS location, timestamps, and user comments in image files. Modern phones embed this data automatically.
Use Python's Pillow library: from PIL import Image; img = Image.open('photo.jpg'); exif = img._getexif(); Look for key 37510 (MakerNote or UserComment) or key 37500 (MakerNote).

solutionSteps: 3. Script reads all EXIF tags and prints them
4. Look for the Comment or UserComment field
5. The flag will be visible in the output

pythonScript.explanation: Teaches EXIF extraction using Pillow. Students learn that images contain hidden metadata that's often overlooked.

challenges.title: Track Changes
challenges.description: Microsoft Office files hide secrets in their metadata. Extract author info, revision history, and custom properties from a Word document (.docx). The flag is in the document properties.
challenges.learningObjective: Understand that .docx files are ZIP archives, read XML metadata, extract document properties
challenges.prerequisite: Python 3 with python-docx: pip install python-docx

hints.text: A .docx file is actually a ZIP archive. You can rename it to .zip and extract it to see the XML inside. The metadata lives in 'word/document.xml' or 'docProps/core.xml'.
Use python-docx library: from docx import Document; doc = Document('file.docx'); props = doc.core_properties; Check props.author, props.subject, props.comments, props.category.

solutionSteps: 4. Look for unusual author, subject, or comments
5. Flag will appear in one of these fields

pythonScript.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from docx import Document

# Solution for Challenge 3: Track Changes
# Extract metadata from Word documents

try:
    doc = Document('document.docx')
    core_props = doc.core_properties
    
    print("\n=== Document Properties ===")
    print(f"Author: {core_props.author}")
    print(f"Subject: {core_props.subject}")
    print(f"Title: {core_props.title}")
    print(f"Comments: {core_props.comments}")
    print(f"Category: {core_props.category}")
    print(f"Keywords: {core_props.keywords}")
    print(f"Last Modified By: {core_props.last_modified_by}")
    print(f"Revision Count: {core_props.revision}")
    
    # Search all properties for flag pattern
    all_props = str(vars(core_props))
    if 'flag{' in all_props:
        print("\n*** FLAG FOUND IN METADATA ***")
        # Extract it
        import re
        matches = re.findall(r'flag\{[^}]+\}', all_props)
        for match in matches:
            print(f"Flag: {match}")
    
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    print("Make sure document.docx exists in the current directory.")
pythonScript.explanation: Shows students that Word files (.docx) are actually XML/ZIP archives, revealing hidden structural data.

challenges.title: Between the Lines
challenges.description: Data can be hidden in the least significant bits (LSB) of image pixels. Extract the flag from a PNG image where each pixel's LSB contains one bit of the flag.
challenges.learningObjective: Understand LSB steganography, learn bitwise operations, extract data from pixel channels
challenges.prerequisite: Python 3 with Pillow: pip install Pillow

hints.text: LSB (Least Significant Bit) steganography hides data in the smallest color values. Example: RGB(255, 128, 64) has LSBs of (1, 0, 0). By collecting LSBs from many pixels, you can reconstruct hidden data.
Extract the red channel's LSB from each pixel: r & 1. Collect these bits in groups of 8 to form ASCII characters. Use chr(int('01101001', 2)) to convert bits to characters.

solutionSteps: 3. Script extracts LSBs from red channel of each pixel

pythonScript.explanation: Teaches students about steganography and bitwise operations. Shows that images contain exploitable patterns.

challenges.title: Can You Hear It?
challenges.description: The flag is hidden in a spectrogram of an audio file. Analyze the frequency content of a WAV file and look for text patterns visible in the spectrogram visualization.
challenges.learningObjective: Understand digital signal processing, spectrograms, frequency domain analysis
challenges.prerequisite: Python 3 with scipy, matplotlib: pip install scipy matplotlib numpy

hints.text: A spectrogram is a visual representation of frequency content over time. Some audio steganography embeds text or patterns directly into the frequency domain, making them visible as shapes or letters when you plot the spectrogram.
Use scipy.signal.spectrogram() to compute frequency data, then plot with matplotlib's pcolormesh(). Save the visualization as an image and inspect it visually for the flag.

solutionSteps: 3. Open the generated 'spectrogram.png' in an image viewer
4. Look for text/patterns in the spectrogram (usually bright areas)
5. Read the flag directly from the visual pattern

pythonScript.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.io import wavfile
from scipy import signal
import numpy as np

# Solution for Challenge 5: Can You Hear It?
# Generate and analyze spectrograms from audio files

try:
    # Read the WAV file
    rate, data = wavfile.read('audio.wav')
    print(f"Sample rate: {rate} Hz")
    print(f"Audio shape: {data.shape}")
    
    # Compute spectrogram
    frequencies, times, Sxx = signal.spectrogram(data, rate)
    
    # Create figure and plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(16, 8))
    plt.pcolormesh(times, frequencies, 10 * np.log10(Sxx + 1e-10), shading='gouraud')
    plt.ylabel('Frequency (Hz)')
    plt.xlabel('Time (sec)')
    plt.title('Spectrogram - Look for text patterns in bright areas')
    plt.colorbar(label='Power (dB)')
    
    # Save and show
    plt.savefig('spectrogram.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    print("\nSpectrogram saved as 'spectrogram.png'")
    print("Open the image and look for text/patterns in the bright regions.")
    plt.show()
    
    # Optional: Try to extract text using OCR (advanced)
    try:
        import pytesseract
        from PIL import Image
        img = Image.open('spectrogram.png')
        text = pytesseract.image_to_string(img)
        print(f"\nOCR extracted text: {text}")
    except:
        print("\nFor automated text extraction, install pytesseract: pip install pytesseract")
    
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    print("Make sure audio.wav exists in the current directory.")
pythonScript.explanation: Introduces DSP concepts and spectral analysis. Shows that audio data is just numbers that can be visualized and analyzed.

challenges.title: Off By One
challenges.description: There's a bug in the provided Python script. Find the off-by-one error and fix it. When you run the corrected code, it will print the flag.
challenges.learningObjective: Learn to debug code, understand loop boundaries, common programming mistakes

hints.text: Off-by-one errors happen with loop boundaries. Check: Does the loop iterate from 0 or 1? Does it go to n or n+1? Are you using '<' or '<=' ?
Look at the condition: 'i < len(secret) - 1'. This skips the last character. Change it to 'i < len(secret)' to include all characters.

solutionSteps: 1. Copy the buggy code (provided in challenge page)
2. Run it and see what output you get
3. Look at the loop condition: 'i < len(secret) - 1'
5. Run again, flag will print correctly

pythonScript.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Challenge 6: Off By One - BUGGY CODE
# Find and fix the bug

secret = "flag{0ff_by_0n3}"

print("=== BUGGY CODE ===")
print("Attempting to print the secret...\n")

# BUG: This condition skips the last character!
for i in range(len(secret)):
    if i < len(secret) - 1:  # <--- THE BUG IS HERE
        print(secret[i], end='')

print("\n\n=== CORRECTED CODE ===")
print("After fixing the bug:\n")

# FIXED: Include all characters
for i in range(len(secret)):
    if i < len(secret):  # <--- FIXED (or just remove the condition entirely)
        print(secret[i], end='')

print("\n")
pythonScript.explanation: Teaches debugging and understanding loop boundaries - a common mistake for beginners.

challenges.title: Brute Force 101
challenges.description: A simple 4-digit PIN protects the vault. Write a brute force script that tries all 10,000 possible combinations (0000-9999) until it finds the correct one. The flag is revealed when you crack the PIN.
challenges.learningObjective: Understand brute force attacks, loops, password cracking basics

hints.text: Brute force means trying every possible combination. For a 4-digit PIN, that's 10^4 = 10,000 possibilities. Use a for loop from 0 to 9999.
Use range(10000) to iterate through all PINs. For each iteration, check if check_pin(pin) returns True. When found, print the flag.

solutionSteps: 2. The script defines check_pin(n) which returns True if n is correct
3. Write a for loop trying all 4-digit combinations
4. When check_pin returns True, print the flag
5. Script will find PIN 7734 and output the flag

pythonScript.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Challenge 7: Brute Force 101
# Crack the 4-digit PIN

def check_pin(pin):
    """Returns True if pin is correct"""
    correct_pin = 7734
    return pin == correct_pin

print("Starting brute force attack on 4-digit PIN...")
print("Trying all combinations from 0000 to 9999...\n")

found = False
attempts = 0

for pin in range(10000):
    attempts += 1
    if check_pin(pin):
        print(f"\n*** PIN FOUND after {attempts} attempts! ***")
        print(f"Correct PIN: {pin:04d}")
        print(f"\nflag{{brut3_f0rce_w0rkz}}")
        found = True
        break
    
    # Print progress every 1000 attempts
    if attempts % 1000 == 0:
        print(f"Tried {attempts} combinations...")

if not found:
    print("PIN not found! (This shouldn't happen)")
pythonScript.explanation: Practical example of how brute force attacks work. Shows both the power and inefficiency of this method.

challenges.title: Layers
challenges.description: The flag is wrapped in three layers of encoding: Hex → ROT13 → Base64. Your task: decode it by reversing the layers. Start with the hex string provided and work backwards.
challenges.learningObjective: Understand common encoding schemes, chain decoding operations, recognize encoding signatures

hints.text: Layers work like Russian nesting dolls. To get the flag: Decode Base64 → Apply ROT13 → Decode Hex. You do the OPPOSITE of encoding.
Python tools: bytes.fromhex(s) for hex, codecs.encode(s, 'rot_13') for ROT13, base64.b64decode(s) for Base64. Chain them in reverse order.

pythonScript.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import base64
import codecs

# Challenge 8: Layers - Encoding/Decoding
# The flag is encoded with: Hex -> ROT13 -> Base64
# We decode in REVERSE order: Base64 -> ROT13 -> Hex

# This is the encoded flag (provided in the challenge)
encoded = "666c61677b6c3433723e645f336e633064316e677d"  # Change to actual value

print("Starting multi-layer decoding...\n")

try:
    print(f"Step 1 (Hex decode): {encoded}")
    hex_decoded = bytes.fromhex(encoded).decode()
    print(f"After hex decode: {hex_decoded}\n")
    
    print(f"Step 2 (ROT13 decode): {hex_decoded}")
    rot13_decoded = codecs.encode(hex_decoded, 'rot_13')
    print(f"After ROT13 decode: {rot13_decoded}\n")
    
    print(f"Step 3 (Base64 decode): {rot13_decoded}")
    final = base64.b64decode(rot13_decoded).decode()
    print(f"FINAL FLAG: {final}\n")
    
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error during decoding: {e}")
    print("\nTroubleshooting:")
    print("- Make sure the encoded string is correct")
    print("- Check that each layer can be decoded")
    print("- Try decoding each layer manually to see where it breaks")
pythonScript.explanation: Shows that encoding ≠ encryption. Stacks common encoding techniques to create obfuscation, not security.

challenges.title: Inspect Me
challenges.description: A web API is leaking the flag in its JSON response. Use browser DevTools to inspect network traffic and find the hidden API call that contains the flag.
challenges.learningObjective: Use browser DevTools Network tab, inspect API responses, understand HTTP requests/responses

hints.text: Open Browser DevTools (F12) → Network tab → Refresh the page → Look for XHR or Fetch requests. The flag might be in the response JSON of an API call the page makes.
Find the API endpoint (e.g., /api/secret or /api/ctf/flag). The response will have a JSON object with keys like 'flag', 'secret', 'data', etc. Copy the flag value.

6. In the 'Response' tab, find the JSON with the flag

challenges.title: The Long Way Round
challenges.description: The ultimate challenge combines TWO previous techniques. First, extract LSB data from an image (Challenge 4). Then, decode the extracted data using Base64 (Challenge 8). The final result is your flag.
challenges.learningObjective: Combine multiple techniques, chain operations, think across domains

hints.text: This is a TWO-STEP challenge. Step 1: Extract LSB from image pixels (like Challenge 4). Step 2: Take the extracted string and Base64 decode it (like Challenge 8). Chain these operations.
The extracted LSB data will look like a Base64 string (contains letters, numbers, +/, =). Decode it using base64.b64decode() to get the final flag.

resources: Combining techniques: Refer to Challenges 4 and 8
solutionSteps: 3. Script extracts LSB from red channel (Challenge 4 technique)

pythonScript.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from PIL import Image
import base64
import re

# Challenge 10: The Long Way Round
# Combines LSB steganography + Base64 decoding

print("=== STEP 1: Extract LSB from image ===")
print("Reading image and extracting LSB data...\n")

try:
    # STEP 1: Extract LSB (same as Challenge 4)
    image = Image.open('final_image.png').convert('RGB')
    pixels = image.load()
    width, height = image.size
    
    bits = []
    for y in range(height):
        for x in range(width):
            r, g, b = pixels[x, y]
            bits.append(str(r & 1))
            if len(bits) >= 512:  # Base64 string is longer
                break
        if len(bits) >= 512:
            break
    
    # Convert bits to ASCII
    extracted = ''
    for i in range(0, len(bits), 8):
        byte = ''.join(bits[i:i+8])
        if len(byte) == 8:
            char = chr(int(byte, 2))
            extracted += char
    
    print(f"Extracted data: {extracted}\n")
    
    # STEP 2: Decode Base64
    print("=== STEP 2: Base64 decode ===")
    print(f"Attempting to Base64 decode...\n")
    
    # Clean up the extracted data (remove non-Base64 chars)
    base64_clean = re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z0-9+/=]', '', extracted)
    
    try:
        flag = base64.b64decode(base64_clean).decode()
        print(f"*** FINAL FLAG: {flag} ***")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Base64 decode failed: {e}")
        print(f"Raw extracted data: {extracted}")
        
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    print("Make sure final_image.png exists in the current directory.")
pythonScript.explanation: Capstone challenge that shows real-world scenarios often involve multiple layers of obfuscation combined.
